beats.story: Why we ran these experiments
beats.title: Can an AI agent engineer a robot?

beats.story: Why we ran these experiments
beats.title: Skills are not jobs

narration.text: Robot AI models are learning skills fast. But a business needs whole jobs done reliably, in its own setting, and its jobs keep changing. Turning skills into reliable work is engineering: watch the failures, find the cause, change the system, prove it. Today, specialists do that by hand, for every change, and that makes automation slow and expensive.

beats.story: Why we ran these experiments
beats.title: The question

narration.text: Mayfly is building robot installations whose engineering is done by AI agents. Before building that on real robots, we tested the core question in simulation: can an agent find out on its own what needs to change, change it, and prove that it works? We ran two experiments, one for each kind of engineering an installation keeps needing. The first: a new job, made from skills the robot already has. Every new product or packing rule asks for a job like this, and today a specialist has to make it reliable. The second: faults we planted in a fleet of robots. When robots that worked yesterday start to fail, someone has to find out why, and repair it.

beats.story: The test bench and the rules
beats.title: The test bench

narration.text: The test bench is a physics simulator with a kitchen scene from a public robotics benchmark. In simulation, every start can be repeated exactly and every motion measured, and the kitchen makes the failures easy to follow. The robot runs X-VLA, an open robot vision-language-action model: it turns camera images and a written instruction into motion. For these experiments we kept it fixed, so every gain comes from the engineering around it.

clips.label: job 1, release, the saved job on start 31, the whole station

beats.story: The test bench and the rules
beats.title: The engineer and its sandbox

narration.text: The engineer is an AI agent in a sandbox. Like a robotics engineer at a desk, it looks at camera frames from its trials and reads the measurements the simulator records: where the hand is, where each object is, what touches what. It writes its own checks, builds programs from the robot's skills and runs experiments. It knows the rules it is graded by, and cannot change them. The faults we planted stay hidden from it, and the exam layouts stay locked away until its solution is final. We built the bench, wrote the requests and fixed the grading. After that, no person took part: the agent chose every experiment and wrote every solution.

beats.story: The test bench and the rules
beats.title: A fair test

narration.text: Each try starts from a stored arrangement of the table: a layout. The agent compares its programs on the same practice layouts. 20 more stay locked away for a final exam it never sees in advance. On those same 20, we also run the plain chain, the skills simply one after the other. That is the baseline. Later, on real robots, the practice layouts will be simulated copies of the real station, and the final exam will take place in the real world.

beats.story: Experiment one: a new job from existing skills
beats.title: Experiment one: the request

narration.text: Experiment one. The request, as a shift lead would write it: bowl on top of the cabinet, middle drawer open, everything at rest, hand clear. The bar: the whole job completed without a failure on at least 18 of 20 fresh layouts.

beats.story: Experiment one: a new job from existing skills
beats.title: Watch it fail

narration.text: Chained plainly, the job falls apart. The drawer skill starts the moment the bowl counts as placed. But the hand still holds the bowl, and drags it off.

beats.title: Measure why

beats.story: Experiment one: a new job from existing skills
beats.title: One change at a time

narration.text: Then it changes one thing at a time, on the same practice layouts. Open the fingers first? They still catch the bowl. Go home first? The way home snags it. What works: let the placement finish, so the hand lets go and lifts, then go home, then open the drawer: 10 of 10 successful jobs.

beats.story: Experiment one: a new job from existing skills
beats.title: The final exam

narration.text: Before the exam, it confirms the program on 20 practice layouts it had never used. 20 of 20. Then the final exam, on the 20 locked layouts. The plain chain gets 1 right. The agent's job: 20 of 20.

beats.story: Experiment one: a new job from existing skills
beats.title: Kept for the next request

narration.text: The job and its check go into the installation's library, ready for the next request. From request to proven job, the agent took 41 minutes.

beats.story: Experiment one: a new job from existing skills
beats.title: A harder job

narration.text: The second request is harder. Two things must end up in place: the plate at the front of the stove, and the bowl on top of the cabinet. The robot has a skill for each: one pushes the plate, the other places the bowl. Chained plainly, the job succeeds on 5 of 20 fresh layouts. The trouble is a pack of cream cheese in the plate's way: the push runs into it, or the hand grabs the cheese instead.

beats.title: The bottleneck moves

beats.story: Experiment one: a new job from existing skills
beats.title: What experiment one showed

narration.text: What did the first experiment show? Twice, a new job failed when the robot's skills were simply chained. Twice, the agent found the physical cause, changed how the job is done, and proved its solution on layouts it had never seen, with no person in the loop. That matters, because this is the engineering that makes every new job slow and expensive today. Here, an agent did it, in 41 and 113 minutes.

beats.story: Experiment two: faults planted in a fleet
beats.title: Experiment two: planted faults

narration.text: Experiment two asks a different question: when working robots start to fail, can the agent find out why? We built a fleet of 12 simulated arms at 3 sites, doing pick-and-place work, and planted problems in it. The agent is told nothing about them. It sees what an operator sees: results, telemetry, change and maintenance logs, and the actions an operator can take.

beats.story: Experiment two: faults planted in a fleet
beats.title: What we planted

narration.text: Here is what we planted. At the first site, the model that drives the robots runs in the customer's distant data centre, and the line adds a delay. The customer requires that link, so it stays. At the second site, one robot's controller is overloaded and falls behind. At the third site, a software update crops part of every camera image before the model sees it. On the same day, a camera's calibration record is rewritten, which changes nothing at all. That one is our false lead.

beats.story: Experiment two: faults planted in a fleet
beats.title: What the agent sees

narration.text: The agent is not told what causes the failures. It sees the operating records. The robots at the first site trail their commands and succeed far less often. One robot at the second site trails just the same. The robots at the third site fail more often than the healthy robots, and the change log shows two changes on the same day. Same symptom, same cause? And which of the two changes is to blame?

beats.story: Experiment two: faults planted in a fleet
beats.title: The agent builds an instrument

narration.text: The task records can't tell the first two apart. So the agent builds an instrument: a small test motion, with the robot's model switched off, timing how each arm follows a command. At the first site, the hand always starts late, by the same amount: a delay on the line. The robot at the second site starts nearly on time, then falls further and further behind: its controller can't keep up. They look alike, but they are two different problems, and they need different repairs.

beats.story: Experiment two: faults planted in a fleet
beats.title: Tested repairs

narration.text: Each repair is tested on its own before it is adopted. The first site's link has to stay, so the agent has the robots skip commands that would be out of date by the time they arrive. It tests three compensation settings and keeps the best. The overloaded controller at the second site is serviced. At the third site, it undoes each of the two changes in a separate test. Rolling back the software update brings the site back. Rolling back the calibration shows no clear effect. So it adopts the software rollback, and leaves the calibration alone.

beats.story: Experiment two: faults planted in a fleet
beats.title: The fleet result

narration.text: Then the test that counts: 576 attempts the agent never saw. As the fleet was, 451 successes. With the agent's 3 changes, 558. From 78% to 97%. Against what we planted: all three problems found, each with a tested repair, and the false lead left alone.

beats.story: What we learned, and what comes next
beats.title: The results

narration.text: In both experiments, the agent did the engineering itself. Two new jobs: from 1 to 20 of 20, and from 5 to 20. A fleet: from 78% to 97%. The robots' vision-language-action model and their overall design stayed the same throughout.

beats.story: What we learned, and what comes next
beats.title: What we learned

narration.text: What we learned: the agent worked like a good engineer. It looked at the evidence, found the physical cause, changed one thing at a time, built a measurement when the records weren't enough, and proved its solutions on cases it had never seen. These were first, compact tests, and in each one the agent carried the investigation through to a working result.

beats.story: What we learned, and what comes next
beats.title: Next: real robots

narration.text: Next, we take this to real robots: a complete packing operation on two-armed mobile robots, where agents engineer new work on the hardware and prove it there. The question we will answer: how much less human work each new job needs, once agents do the engineering.

beats.story: What we learned, and what comes next
beats.title: What it means

narration.text: That is what Mayfly is building: robot installations where taking on new work is part of the product, because agents do the engineering.
